questions.question: You have a stream of observations, the actions you took, and a scalar reward — no labels anywhere. What has to be added before you can reason about it mathematically?
options: A labeled dataset pairing each observation with the correct action to take
A tuple of states, actions, transitions, rewards, and a discount
A loss function comparing predicted reward to actual reward
A larger network, so the reward signal has capacity to fit
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning is handed no supervision, so the structure has to come from the problem itself. The five-object MDP tuple is what turns "what I saw / did / got" into objects you can take expectations over.

questions.question: Your agent needs the last three camera frames to decide what to do next. What does the lesson say this tells you?
options: The discount is set too low for the task's horizon
The Markov property genuinely fails here, so an MDP cannot model the task
The state representation is incomplete, not the method
The reward function has become non-stationary
questions.explanation: Markov is a property of the state you chose, not of the world. Stacking frames or carrying a recurrent state restores it without changing the algorithm.

questions.question: The lesson ties the discount to an effective horizon of roughly 1/(1-γ). What does γ = 0.999 buy?
options: About 10 steps
About 100 steps
An unbounded horizon — only γ = 1 exactly is myopic
About 1000 steps
questions.explanation: Each extra nine multiplies 1/(1-γ) by ten. That is why control tasks sit at 0.95–0.99 and long-horizon strategy games reach 0.999.

questions.question: What do the Bellman equations do to the expected return?
options: Replace it with the undiscounted sum so γ can be dropped
Split it into this step's reward plus the discounted successor value
Bound it above by the largest single-step reward in the MDP
Approximate it with a function approximator so large state spaces stay tractable
questions.explanation: That recursive split is what makes the return computable one step at a time. Every method in the phase either iterates it, samples it, or bootstraps one step of it.

questions.question: You want to compare two candidate opening moves from the same board position, assuming the same policy is followed afterwards. Which object answers that directly?
options: V^π(s), the state value
The transition function P(s' | s, a)
Q^π(s, a), the action value
The discount γ and the resulting horizon
questions.explanation: Q conditions on a specific first action and only then follows π, which is exactly the comparison being asked for. V has already averaged the first action away.

questions.question: A boat-racing agent circles forever collecting powerups and never finishes the race. Which diagnosis does the lesson give?
options: The reward was written against a proxy, not the target outcome
γ was set too close to 1 for an infinite-horizon task
The state is non-Markovian, so credit assignment cannot work at all
The reward range is too wide and the gradients exploded
questions.explanation: The agent optimized exactly what it was given; the specification was wrong, not the optimizer. The fix lives in the reward definition, not in the algorithm.
